objectives: To understand how to make strong passwords, keep them secret and what to do if an account is at risk

Most: make a strong passphrase from three random words
Some: explain what to do if a password is shared or an account is hacked

keywords.def: a secret word that protects an account
a password made of several random words
a second check, such as a code
someone getting into your account without permission

hook.a: 'cactus-lantern-river': it's longer and not linked to you, so it's much harder to guess.

islamicLink.text: An account is an amanah (trust); keeping it safe protects you and others.

starter.q: Best chart for change over time is ...

starter.a: The line along the side or bottom of a chart.

teach.heading: Strong password rules
bullets: Not your name, birthday or pet
Never shared, except with a parent

teach.heading: If something goes wrong
cycle: Tell your teacher if it's a school account

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: A friend asks for your password 'just to help'. You ...
options: say no and tell a parent

practice.q: Make a passphrase from three random words (don't use a real one you use!).

exit.q: The safest password here is ...

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Variables in games and e-bullying
lessons.title: E-bullying: respond, block and report
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a mean comment online less hurtful than one said face to face? Why?
objectives: To understand how to respond to e-bullying safely by blocking, reporting and telling
successCriteria: All: say what e-bullying is
Most: put the steps 'stop, block, screenshot, tell' in order
Some: explain how a bystander can help someone being bullied online
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: bullying and asking for help
lessons.smsc: Moral: speaking good or staying silent

keywords.def: hurting someone on purpose, again and again
stop someone contacting you
tell the website or school about something wrong
a picture of the screen kept as evidence

hook.text: Is a mean comment online less hurtful than one said face to face? Why?
hook.a: No: it can be seen by many, saved and shared, and it can follow you home.

islamicLink.text: Allah tells the believers not to mock one another or call each other by offensive names (al-Hujurat 49:11). The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent' (al-Bukhari and Muslim). This applies to every message we type.

starter.a: A named store for a value that can change.
options: A named store for a value

starter.q: Name one thing never to post in the class chat.
starter.a: A password, an address or anything unkind.
A fake message that tries to trick you.

teach.heading: What is e-bullying?
bullets: Sharing pictures or words to upset
teach.note: It is bullying using devices. It is never the victim's fault.

teach.heading: Stop, block, screenshot, tell
teach.note: In Teams: tell your teacher at once; the school can see and deal with chat messages. Do not delete evidence.

teach.heading: Be an upstander
bullets: Do not like or share it
Send a kind message to the person
teach.note: A bystander watches; an upstander helps safely.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Someone keeps posting mean comments on your shared Scratch project. First step?
options: Do not reply; screenshot and tell a trusted adult
check.why: Replying can make it worse; evidence and an adult can stop it. Ignoring forever lets it carry on.

practice.q: Put in order: tell, block, stop, screenshot.
practice.model: Teacher explains each step's reason: stop (do not feed it), block (it cannot reach you), screenshot (proof), tell (an adult can act).

practice.a: Not on its own, but it is still wrong; repeated, on purpose, it is bullying.

practice.q: Name two trusted adults you could tell.
practice.a: For example: a parent and my class teacher.

independent.q: Core: Read the three scenarios. For each, write what to do using the four steps.
independent.a: Each answer uses stop, block, screenshot, tell; scenario 3 also includes being an upstander.

independent.q: Extend: Write a kind message an upstander could send to someone who was bullied, in the portal response box.
independent.a: For example: 'I saw what happened. It was not okay. I am here, and I have told a teacher.'

independent.q: Stretch: Discuss in your breakout pair: why might someone not tell? What would help them tell?
independent.a: Fear or embarrassment; knowing adults will help and it is not their fault.

exit.q: A screenshot is useful because... A) it is fun B) it keeps evidence C) it hides the message
Big question: is a mean comment online less hurtful? Give one reason.
exit.a: No: it can be seen by many people and saved.

lessons.homework: Make a 'Stop, block, screenshot, tell' poster (words and symbols, no people) for your home learning space.
lessons.send: SEND: four step cards with symbols. EAL: block, report, evidence. Stretch: research how to report on one app with a parent.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Variables in games and e-bullying
lessons.title: What is a variable? Score and lives
lessons.bigQuestion: In a game your score goes 0, 1, 2, 3... Where does the computer keep that number?
objectives: To understand that a variable stores a value that can change while a program runs
successCriteria: All: name a variable in a game (score, lives, time)
Most: say how a variable's value changes during a game
Some: create a variable in Scratch and set its starting value
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: algebra, a letter standing for a number

keywords.def: a named store for a value that can change
what is stored in the variable right now
a variable that counts points
an object we program in Scratch

hook.text: In a game your score goes 0, 1, 2, 3... Where does the computer keep that number?
hook.a: In a variable: a labelled box in memory whose value changes.

starter.q: Which is selection? A) repeat 10 B) if... then C) move 10 steps
What should you never share online?
Who do you tell if something online worries you?

teach.heading: E-safety recap
teach.note: Class studio is set so only the class sees projects (TO CONFIRM settings).

teach.heading: A labelled box
teach.note: Picture a box labelled 'score' with a 3 inside. Add 1: now 4.

teach.heading: Variables in Scratch
bullets: set score to 0 at the start
teach.note: Model: green flag, set score to 0. The variable monitor shows on the stage.

code.text:
when green flag clicked
set score to 0
set lives to 3
code.output: The stage shows score 0 and lives 3.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: score is 5. The program runs 'change score by 1' twice. What is score now?

practice.q: Start: score 0. Catch, catch, catch. What is score?
practice.model: Teacher writes the value after each event: 0, 1, 2, 3.

practice.q: Start: lives 3. Miss, miss. What is lives?
What is the difference between 'set score to 0' and 'change score by 1'?
practice.a: Set replaces the value; change adds to it.

independent.q: Core: Make a new Scratch project with a Bowl sprite and an Apple sprite (delete the cat). Create the variables score and lives and set them on green flag.
independent.a: set score to 0, set lives to 3 on green flag.
independent.model: Teacher makes 'score', sets it to 0, then pupils make 'lives'.

independent.q: Extend: Fill a value table for 6 events of your own (catch or miss).
independent.a: Any table where score goes up by 1 on a catch and lives down by 1 on a miss.

independent.q: Stretch: What should happen when lives reaches 0? Write it as an if... then rule.
independent.a: IF lives = 0 THEN say 'Game over' and stop all.

exit.q: A variable... A) never changes B) stores a value that can change C) is a sprite
exit.a: B) stores a value that can change
options: Stores a value that can change

exit.q: Name two variables a game might use.

lessons.homework: Think of a game you know (board or screen). List its variables and how each one changes.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Variables in games and e-bullying
lessons.title: Changing a variable when a sprite is clicked
lessons.bigQuestion: A clicker counter at the masjid door counts people coming in. How would you program one?
objectives: To understand how an event changes the value of a variable
successCriteria: All: use 'when this sprite clicked' to start a script
Most: change score by 1 each click and show it
Some: reset the variable at the start and explain why
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: counting dhikr after salah, like the tally counter

keywords.def: something that happens and starts a script, like a click
add to a variable's value
pressing the mouse button on something
what the variable holds now

hook.text: A clicker counter at the masjid door counts people coming in. How would you program one?
hook.a: Each click (event) changes a count variable by 1; the start sets it to 0.

starter.q: 'set' a variable means... A) add to it B) replace its value C) delete it
score is 4, change score by 1. Now?
Name the category for variables in Scratch.

starter.a: Something that starts a script, like the green flag.

teach.heading: Events start scripts
teach.note: Yellow Events category. Each event is a 'hat' block.

teach.heading: Click to score
teach.note: On the Apple sprite.

code.text:
when green flag clicked
set score to 0

when this sprite clicked
change score by 1
go to random position
code.output: Each click adds 1 and the apple jumps somewhere new.

teach.heading: Why reset?
bullets: Score carries on from last game
teach.note: Show the bug: run twice without reset.

misconception.wrong: The score starts at 0 by itself every time
misconception.right: A variable keeps its last value until you set it again, so set it to 0 at the start

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: You click the apple 4 times, press the green flag, then click 2 times. What is score?
check.why: The green flag sets score to 0, then two clicks make it 2.

practice.q: Add 'when this sprite clicked, change score by 1' to the Apple.
practice.a: The score goes up by 1 per click.
practice.model: Teacher drags the hat block, snaps 'change score by 1', clicks the apple three times and reads the monitor.

practice.q: Add 'go to random position' after the change. What does it do?
practice.a: The apple jumps to a new place after each click.

practice.q: Why do we put 'set score to 0' under the green flag?
practice.a: So each new game starts from 0.

independent.q: Core: Make a 'click the apple' game: score up by 1 per click, apple jumps, score reset on the flag.
independent.a: Two scripts on the Apple: flag (set 0) and click (change by 1, random position).
independent.model: Teacher shows the flag script first.

independent.q: Extend: Add a Bowl sprite that takes away a point when clicked by mistake.
independent.a: Bowl: when this sprite clicked, change score by -1.

independent.q: Stretch: Make the apple say 'Well done!' when score reaches 10.
independent.a: if score = 10 then say 'Well done!' (inside the click script).

exit.q: Which block is an event? A) change score by 1 B) when this sprite clicked C) go to random position
Why must a game reset its score at the start?
exit.a: A variable keeps its last value, so without a reset it carries on from the last game.

lessons.homework: Write the two scripts for a counter that counts how many times you say 'SubhanAllah' after salah (click to add, flag to reset).
lessons.send: SEND: scripts given as screenshots to copy. EAL: event, click, change. Stretch: a 'best score' variable.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Variables in games and e-bullying
lessons.title: A catching game: selection and score
lessons.bigQuestion: In a catching game, how does the computer know you caught the apple?
objectives: To understand how selection checks a condition to change a variable in a game
successCriteria: All: make an apple fall down the stage
Most: use 'if touching Bowl then change score by 1'
Some: reset the apple to the top after a catch or a miss
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: coordinates (x and y) in all four quadrants

keywords.def: choosing what to do with if... then
a true or false check, like 'touching Bowl?'
the block that runs code only when the condition is true
play the game to check it works

hook.text: In a catching game, how does the computer know you caught the apple?
hook.a: It keeps checking a condition: is the apple touching the bowl? If so, add a point.

starter.q: What starts a script when a sprite is clicked?
score is 7, change score by -1. Now?

starter.a: A question that is true or false.

starter.q: Why reset score at the start?

teach.heading: Make it fall
bullets: Start at the top: go to x: random, y: 170
teach.note: y is up and down; negative change moves down.

teach.heading: Did we catch it?
teach.note: Selection inside the forever loop.

code.text:
when green flag clicked
set score to 0
go to x: (pick random -200 to 200) y: 170
forever
  change y by -5
  if touching Bowl? then
    change score by 1
    go to x: (pick random -200 to 200) y: 170
  end
code.output: Apples fall; each catch adds 1 and the apple restarts at the top.

teach.heading: Move the bowl
teach.note: Two short scripts on the Bowl.

model.problem: Make the bowl move left and right.
steps: when right arrow key pressed: change x by 20
when left arrow key pressed: change x by -20
model.answer: Two key-press scripts changing x by 20 and -20

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: The apple falls but the score never changes. Most likely bug?
options: The if is outside the forever loop
check.why: Outside the loop, the condition is checked only once at the start, before any catch.

practice.q: Build the falling script on the Apple.
practice.a: go to top, forever change y by -5.
practice.model: Teacher builds the start position and the forever loop, then runs it.

practice.q: Add the if touching Bowl block inside the loop.
practice.a: if touching Bowl? then change score by 1, go to top.

practice.q: Add arrow-key scripts to the Bowl.
practice.a: right: change x by 20; left: change x by -20.

independent.q: Core: Finish the catching game and test it 5 times. Write the scores.
independent.a: A working game; five test scores recorded.
independent.model: Teacher plays once and talks through what to watch for.

independent.q: Extend: Add a second 'if': if y position < -170 then change lives by -1 and go to the top.
independent.a: A miss below the bowl loses a life.

independent.q: Stretch: Make the apple fall faster as score goes up. Which block do you change?
independent.a: Use change y by (-5 - score / 2), or a 'speed' variable.

exit.q: 'if touching Bowl? then' is... A) a loop B) selection C) an event
Why must the if block be inside the forever loop?
exit.a: So the condition is checked again and again as the apple falls.

lessons.homework: Write the scripts for your game on paper and label one loop, one selection and one variable.
lessons.send: SEND: a half-built project to complete. EAL: fall, touching, if, condition. Stretch: speed variable.

keywords.def: a variable that counts time
find and fix mistakes
a mistake in a program
words shown to the player

hook.text: Why do most games have an end? What decides when your game is over?

starter.q: Where must the 'if touching' block go?
lives is 1. The apple is missed. lives now?

starter.a: Choosing what to do with if... then.

teach.heading: A countdown timer
bullets: repeat until time = 0: wait 1, change time by -1
teach.note: Put the timer on the Stage, not a sprite.

code.text:
when green flag clicked
set time to 30
repeat until time = 0
  wait 1 seconds
  change time by -1
end
broadcast game over

teach.heading: Game over
teach.note: Make a text sprite with the Paint tool (letters only).

teach.heading: Two ways to end
teach.note: Selection: if lives = 0 then broadcast game over.

teach.heading: Test plan
teach.note: Model one row.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: The timer keeps going below 0. Best fix?
check.why: A forever loop never stops; 'repeat until time = 0' stops at 0.

practice.q: Add the countdown timer to the Stage.
practice.a: set time to 30; repeat until time = 0 (wait 1, change time by -1); broadcast game over.
practice.model: Teacher builds it and watches the monitor count down.

practice.q: Add 'when I receive game over: show, stop all' to a text sprite.
practice.a: The game shows 'Game over' and stops.

independent.q: Core: Add game over for lives = 0 too, then run the 3-row test plan and fill it in.
independent.a: if lives = 0 then broadcast game over; test plan completed.
independent.model: Teacher completes row 1 of the test plan live.

independent.q: Extend: Swap projects with the class studio and test a partner's game. Write one kind, specific comment.
independent.a: For example: 'The timer works well; the apple could start in more places.'

independent.q: Stretch: Show the final score on the game over screen.
independent.a: say (join 'Score: ' score).

exit.q: Which block stops the timer at 0? A) forever B) repeat until time = 0 C) wait 1
Big question: what decides when your game is over?
exit.a: Selection on variables: when time or lives reaches 0, the game broadcasts game over.

lessons.title: 3D modelling basics: a Victorian building
lessons.bigQuestion: How could you make a chimney or a window using only simple shapes like boxes and cylinders?
objectives: To understand how 3D models are built from shapes that can be moved, resized and grouped
successCriteria: All: place and resize a 3D shape
Most: combine shapes to make a simple building
Some: use a hole shape and grouping to add windows
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Victorian Britain (factories, terraced houses, railways)
lessons.smsc: Cultural: Victorian buildings in our history topic

keywords.def: having length, width and height
a representation of a real object
the flat surface you build on
join shapes into one object

hook.text: How could you make a chimney or a window using only simple shapes like boxes and cylinders?
hook.a: A tall box or cylinder for the chimney; a 'hole' box cut into the wall for a window.

starter.q: What do you do if your account is hacked?

independent.q: Build a Victorian house or factory with walls, roof, chimney and at least two windows; save and share a screenshot to the portal.
independent.a: A recognisable model with grouped windows.
